records.title: What Is Cleaning Chemistry?
records.excerpt: An introduction to the main ideas behind professional cleaning formulations and how different ingredient groups contribute to cleaning performance.
records.content_html:
Cleaning chemistry explains how a formulation interacts with soils, water and surfaces. Professional cleaners may contain several ingredient groups, each contributing a different function.

Why cleaning chemistry matters

Understanding basic chemistry helps users compare products by intended application rather than by appearance or a single property.

Main formulation components

Depending on the product, a formulation may include surfactants, builders, solvents, enzymes, oxidising agents, disinfectant actives or other functional ingredients.

Product selection

The appropriate product depends on the soil, surface, process and controlled product information. No single chemical property describes overall cleaning performance.
records.seo_title: What Is Cleaning Chemistry? | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Learn the basic principles of cleaning chemistry, including how formulations interact with soils, surfaces, water and different ingredient groups.

records.title: How Cleaning Products Remove Soil
records.excerpt: A practical overview of the different mechanisms cleaning formulations use to loosen, suspend and remove soils from surfaces.
records.content_html:
Cleaning products work by helping separate soil from a surface so it can be removed through the cleaning process.

Soil and surface interactions

Different soils behave differently depending on their composition and the material they are attached to.

Role of formulation

Surfactants, solvents, builders and other ingredients can support wetting, soil release, suspension and removal.

Why one cleaner does not fit all

A formulation suited to one type of soil or surface may not be suitable for another, which is why intended use and compatibility information matter.
records.seo_title: How Cleaning Products Remove Soil | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Understand how cleaning products help loosen, suspend and remove soils and why different formulations suit different cleaning tasks.

records.title: What Is pH in Cleaning Chemicals?
records.excerpt: A clear explanation of pH in cleaning chemistry and why acidic, neutral and alkaline formulations behave differently.
records.content_html:
pH describes whether a water-based solution is acidic, neutral or alkaline. In professional cleaning, it provides useful context about the general character of a formulation.

The pH scale

A value around 7 is neutral, lower values are acidic and higher values are alkaline.

Why pH matters

pH can influence how a cleaner interacts with certain soils and materials, but it does not describe the complete formulation.

Surface compatibility

Surface compatibility depends on the full product formulation and the material being cleaned, not on pH alone.
records.seo_title: What Is pH in Cleaning Chemicals? | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Learn what pH means in cleaning chemicals and how acidic, neutral and alkaline formulations relate to soils and surface compatibility.

records.title: Acidic vs Alkaline Cleaners
records.excerpt: A comparison of acidic and alkaline cleaning chemistry, including the broad types of soils each is commonly associated with.
records.content_html:
Acidic and alkaline cleaners represent two broad chemistry families used for different cleaning challenges.

Acidic cleaners

Acidic formulations are commonly associated with mineral deposits, scale and some inorganic soils.

Alkaline cleaners

Alkaline formulations are commonly associated with grease, oils and heavier organic soils.

Choosing between them

The appropriate choice depends on the soil, material and intended application described in controlled product information.
records.seo_title: Acidic vs Alkaline Cleaners | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Compare acidic and alkaline cleaners, the soils they are commonly associated with, and why surface compatibility matters.

records.title: Does Higher pH Mean a Stronger Cleaner?
records.excerpt: Why pH alone does not measure cleaning strength, cleaning performance or overall formulation effectiveness.
records.content_html:
A higher pH does not automatically mean a cleaner is more effective. pH describes acidity or alkalinity, not total cleaning performance.

What pH tells you

pH gives information about the acid-base character of a water-based solution.

What pH does not tell you

It does not describe surfactant system, solvent content, builders, enzymes or other formulation choices.

Better product comparison

Products should be compared by intended application, soil type, material compatibility and technical documentation rather than pH alone.
records.seo_title: Does Higher pH Mean a Stronger Cleaner? | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Find out why higher pH does not necessarily mean stronger cleaning performance and what matters more when comparing cleaners.

records.title: What Are Surfactants?
records.excerpt: An introduction to surfactants and their role in wetting, soil removal, emulsification and cleaning formulations.
records.content_html:
Surfactants are ingredients used in many cleaning formulations to change how water interacts with surfaces and soils.

Wetting

Surfactants can help a cleaning solution spread across a surface more effectively.

Soil removal

They can support the separation of certain soils from surfaces and help keep removed material suspended.

Different surfactant types

Different surfactant classes have different properties, so formulations are designed around the requirements of the intended application.
records.meta_description: Learn what surfactants are and how they support wetting, soil removal and emulsification in professional cleaning formulations.

records.title: How Surfactants Help Water Spread
records.excerpt: A simple explanation of wetting and why surfactants can help cleaning solutions make better contact with surfaces.
records.content_html:
Water does not always spread evenly across a surface. Surfactants can change that behaviour and improve wetting.

Surface tension

Surface tension affects how water forms droplets and spreads across materials.

Wetting action

Surfactants can reduce surface tension, allowing a solution to contact more of the surface.

Why wetting matters

Better contact can support the cleaning process, although overall performance still depends on the complete formulation and cleaning method.
records.seo_title: How Surfactants Help Water Spread | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Learn how surfactants affect surface tension and help cleaning solutions spread more effectively across surfaces.

records.title: What Is Water Hardness?
records.excerpt: An introduction to water hardness and why dissolved minerals can influence cleaning, scale formation and product performance.
records.content_html:
Water hardness refers mainly to dissolved minerals such as calcium and magnesium in water.

Why water hardness matters

Mineral content can influence scale formation, rinsing behaviour and the way some cleaning formulations perform.

Hard water and scale

As water evaporates or conditions change, mineral deposits can accumulate on surfaces and equipment.

Product formulation

Professional formulations may be designed with water conditions in mind, which is why technical product information is important.
records.seo_title: What Is Water Hardness? | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Learn what water hardness is and how dissolved minerals can affect cleaning performance, rinsing and scale formation.

records.title: How Hard Water Affects Cleaning
records.excerpt: How mineral content in water can affect scale, residue, rinsing and the performance of some cleaning systems.
records.content_html:
Hard water can affect cleaning because dissolved minerals interact with surfaces, residues and some formulation components.

Scale and deposits

Minerals can contribute to visible deposits on fixtures, equipment and other surfaces.

Cleaning performance

The effect of hard water varies by formulation and process, so product documentation should be used when evaluating performance.

System-level considerations

Water quality is one part of the wider cleaning system alongside product chemistry, equipment, method and surface condition.
records.seo_title: How Hard Water Affects Cleaning | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Understand how hard water can influence scale, residue, rinsing and the performance of professional cleaning systems.

records.title: Why Scale Forms on Surfaces
records.excerpt: A practical explanation of how dissolved minerals can leave deposits and why scale commonly appears around water-exposed surfaces.
records.content_html:
Scale commonly forms when dissolved minerals in water become concentrated and remain on a surface after water evaporates or conditions change.

Where scale appears

Deposits often become visible in areas repeatedly exposed to water, especially where evaporation is frequent.

Why it builds up

Repeated wetting and drying can gradually increase mineral deposits if they are not removed through appropriate maintenance.

Surface considerations

Different materials respond differently to cleaning chemistry, so scale-removal decisions should be based on surface compatibility and controlled product information.
records.seo_title: Why Scale Forms on Surfaces | Alle's ClinX
records.meta_description: Learn why mineral scale forms on water-exposed surfaces and how water hardness contributes to visible deposits over time.
